utterances.text: We were visiting him at Meljine, and because of that, I assume that his command was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Up to the end of your mission, you assumed that his command was there?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And where was Admiral Jokic's command?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know any other place, apart from Meljine, with which you had communication on the territory of the Republic of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how did you then attempt to communicate or meet representatives of the JNA? Who did you try to contact, where?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I did not take part in the arranging of these meetings, and I don't know how they were arranged. I'm thinking especially about the meeting on the 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who, then, organised it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Miso organise it?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me once again who went to meet General Strugar and Admiral Jokic on the 28th of October?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bondioli, as the leader of our team, Mr. Haupt, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any special task that you were given by Mr. Bondioli in connection with this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bondioli keep his own personal notes at that meeting, or some sort of minutes?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And your colleague, Mr. Haupt?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't know either, concerning him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you keep any minutes or notes at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: No, not except for the notes I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When exactly did you write down the notes relating to the 28th of October?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Either at the meeting or immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you leave open the possibility that it could have been after the meeting that you wrote down these notes? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember if it was at the meeting or immediately after, more or less. So more or less, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the meeting, while you were talking with the JNA representatives, were you able to see your colleagues from the mission? Were they within your sight?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Yes. We were sitting all of us at the same table, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see whether the ambassador, Bondioli, was taking down notes at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: On the 8th of December, you said that JNA officers came to see the Old Town, and in Exhibit P24, which has four photographs, on the third photograph, you said that only the person in the white coat on that photograph is a member, or rather, a representative of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: He's the only person about whom I'm able to say that he was one of these persons, to my knowledge. There were several -- there were some persons; how many, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: No. I took that photo myself, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How is it possible that you don't know how many JNA officers came to see the Old Town? Because after these events of the 6th of December --

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Well, it's a long time ago. At that time, I probably knew it, but I have forgotten it, simply. It's 12 1/2 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how, then, you were able to recall when making your statement to the investigators that there were two JNA officers? This is not in your notes and you can't remember it now. How, then, were you able to recall it, based on your notes, when giving a statement in April 2002? You said there were two JNA officers, no more, no less. Did someone help you?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Of course I am. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why -- how come you're so sure all of a sudden? This is the most certain reply I've had from you today, that nobody helped you when you were making your statement?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Because this is my statement and only my statement, of course, and it -- probably I'm sure that I -- it's written there that I said that there were two of them, and it's two years ago, and so it seems at that time that I could recall in my memory that there were two of them. But I'm not able to establish that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain on the basis of what you were able to recall back then that there were two of them? Because 10 years had elapsed, or 11 at that time.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I'm not able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether these officers took photographs or made notes when making a tour of the Old Town? Because you said they went round the most part of the Old Town and that you probably showed them some damage. So did they write down any notes? Did they take any photographs or make any sort of record during their visit?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I only knew -- know what is written in my notes, that where I say about them, that they were photographers. And so this must mean that they had some equipment with them, but I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there only two officers making this tour, or don't you know how many officers there were? Were there photographers in their team or not? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND
utterances.text: I don't remember anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether it's a good time to break for the day. Maybe the witness will remember more tomorrow. If this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you give me some indication, Mr. Rodic, of how much longer you would expect to be with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am bearing in mind that the witness has to leave by 4.00 p.m. tomorrow, if I'm well informed, and I will certainly finish my examination bearing this in mind, in time to leave time for my learned friends for another 15 or 20 minutes of examination, if this is enough, redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm asking the question because you've already spent over half an hour longer in cross-examination than the examination-in-chief took, and we are now watching time. So I would be very grateful if you'd be very conscious of time tomorrow. Don't use 4.00 as the target. Try and finish much earlier than that, if we're to move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm greatly encouraged by that, Mr. Rodic. I think we're gradually getting into a better flow of things. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please allow me to address you, very briefly, in connection with something I mentioned on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Is it necessary that the witness remain doing any ancillary matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not necessary. If he wishes to get away now -- we were told it would be a brief address. Would you like to leave now? The situation has been reached, Mr. Brolund, that we will adjourn for the evening, and you are asked to return to complete your evidence tomorrow afternoon, in time, we are assured, for you to get away. If you wish to leave the courtroom now, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave: In accordance with what we said on Friday about the medical examination of our client, the expert who is to examine him arrived in The Hague today. When we talked to the expert immediately before today's session, she said she needed about 12 working hours in order to conduct the examination. In accordance with Your Honours' guidance on Friday, we arranged for her to do the first part tomorrow, from 9.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m. The doctor is to continue on Wednesday at 7.00. My question is: In view of the fact that visits are allowed in the Detention Unit only from 9.00 a.m. onwards, would it be possible for the Trial Chamber to use its influence and authority to ask or influence for the possibility of the doctor to see the accused before 9.00 a.m. in the morning, so that the examination can be completed without infringing on the usual trial time in the afternoon? Or is there a possibility of, with your assistance, our expert seeing the accused earlier in the morning, in order not to lose time, the trial time that we need in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is unlikely at this hour that it will be possible for us to arrange for the visit to commence earlier tomorrow morning, because it is such a short time. It would be possible, though, for us to try to ensure - I can't say that it will happen, but we will endeavour to enable an earlier start on Wednesday morning and, if necessary, Thursday morning. That will depend on the arrangements that are in place in the Detention Centre and whether it will be possible to enable some flexibility there. So we'll do what we can, but by the sound of it, it will be possible, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, for your medical expert to complete her examination without infringing on court time. But we will do what can be done to enable her to have longer periods in the morning, on Wednesday and, if necessary, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course it would be most logical for her to continue on the Thursday. However, according to the doctor's words, the nature of her examination requires that there be a seven-hour period, a continuous seven-hour period for the examination to take place, which is why she would have to come to the Detention Unit at 7.00 or 8.00 a.m. in order to complete the examination by 2.00 p.m., when the accused has to be in this courtroom. This is the reason for my request. Otherwise, she would be able to continue on Thursday. But she said she had to conduct the examination in -- over a continuous seven-hour period, and we need this time on Wednesday. I will see with the Detention Unit whether this is possible at all, and of course we cannot expect a reply from you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Petrovic, but we will certainly communicate with the Detention Unit and encourage, within the scope of what is possible, the prospect of an early start on Wednesday morning. If you are saying that there must be a seven-hour continuous period, we would like to receive from the doctor tomorrow, in writing, some account of the nature of the examination that would require a continuous period of seven hours, which seems unusual, in my limited appreciation of these matters. And if it is to be the case that there is to be any intrusion into the afternoon's sitting time on Wednesday, we will certainly need to see that there was justification for that in a detailed written report from the doctor as to the nature of the examination. Well, I think that's as far as we can take this matter at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, just very briefly: The Defence, bearing this in mind, is prepared to organise this as follows. Two or three hours on Wednesday, we can continue without the presence of the accused in the courtroom, without upsetting our usual schedule. The Defence and the accused are willing to agree to this also. If there is no other way, we propose that the first few hours on Wednesday we work without -- in the absence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that indication, Mr. Petrovic. That is a most unusual course and one we'd prefer to avoid, if possible. We'll judge from events tomorrow whether that is something that need to be considered seriously or not. Thank you, though, for the indication. Could I mention one matter, Mr. Rodic or Mr. Petrovic? We're waiting on your response to the application which the Prosecution made to add new documents to the Rule 65 ter list. I wonder if that response is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have not done this in writing. We expected to have an opportunity to discuss several housekeeping matters before the Chamber, as we requested on Friday. We have no objection to this course, and we are willing to accept this as regards the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. So we can proceed on the basis, then, that there is no objection to the Prosecution's application; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with regard to the Prosecution's application, this is correct. Should there be another application in future, we will address it at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would indicate that we are prepared to hear you briefly, later in the week, at a convenient time - we'll just judge how witnesses are going and when there's a convenient time of five or so minutes - on the motion for the extension of time for filing the expert report issue. So if you could be sure to be ready, and we'll hear you when an opportunity arises on that. Thank you, then, everybody. We will adjourn for the night now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of January 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.
